subject: Anatomy
subtopic: Gross anatomy, histological organization and immune surveillance
concept: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs positioned along lymphatic vessels that filter lymph and provide organized sites for antigen presentation and adaptive immune responses.

content.definition: A lymph node is a small, encapsulated secondary lymphoid organ located along lymphatic vessels. It receives lymph through afferent lymphatic vessels, filters its contents, and returns lymph through efferent lymphatic vessels.
content.explanation: The lymph node is organized so that lymph-borne antigens, antigen-presenting cells, and lymphocytes meet in specialized compartments. B-cell follicles are concentrated in the cortex, T cells and dendritic cells in the paracortex, and plasma cells, macrophages, medullary cords and sinuses in the medulla.
content.mechanism: Lymph from peripheral tissues enters through afferent lymphatics and reaches the subcapsular sinus. It then passes through cortical/trabecular and medullary sinus pathways toward the efferent lymphatic vessel. Antigens and antigen-presenting cells are sampled along this route. Naive lymphocytes also enter from the blood through high endothelial venules in the paracortex. Appropriate antigen recognition activates B- and T-cell responses, while activated B cells can differentiate into plasma cells and memory B cells.
content.structure: A typical lymph node is bean-shaped and enclosed by a connective-tissue capsule. Trabeculae extend inward. The parenchyma is classically divided into cortex, paracortex and medulla. The cortex contains lymphoid follicles, usually B-cell rich; the paracortex is the principal T-cell zone and contains high endothelial venules; the medulla contains medullary cords and medullary sinuses. The concave hilum is associated with efferent lymphatics and blood vessels.
content.function: Major functions include filtration of lymph, antigen capture and processing, immune surveillance, organization of B- and T-cell interactions, and support of adaptive immune responses. Lymph nodes also provide a route through which lymph returns toward the venous circulation.
content.clinical_relevance: Lymph nodes are important in regional infections, reactive lymphadenopathy, lymphoma, metastatic cancer, and immune responses. Their predictable drainage patterns make regional lymph-node examination clinically useful.
content.diagnosis: Lymph-node abnormalities may be evaluated by physical examination, imaging, cytology or biopsy, with histopathology, immunophenotyping, flow cytometry and molecular testing selected according to the clinical question.
content.treatment: Treatment is directed at the underlying cause, such as infection, inflammatory disease, lymphoma, or metastatic malignancy; the node itself is not treated as a single disease entity.
high_yield: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs, unlike the thymus and bone marrow, which are primary lymphoid organs.
Afferent lymphatic vessels enter the convex surface of a lymph node; efferent lymphatic vessels leave at the hilum.
Lymph flow proceeds through the subcapsular sinus and deeper sinus pathways toward the efferent lymphatic vessel.
The cortex contains B-cell-rich lymphoid follicles.
The paracortex is the major T-cell zone and contains high endothelial venules (HEVs), which permit lymphocyte entry from blood.
The medulla contains medullary cords and medullary sinuses; plasma cells are prominent in the cords.
Lymph nodes filter lymph and provide organized sites for antigen presentation and lymphocyte activation.
Secondary follicles develop germinal centers after appropriate antigenic stimulation.

terminology.etymology: Lymph derives from Latin lympha, water/clear fluid; node derives from Latin nodus, knot.
terminology.notes: A secondary lymphoid organ positioned along lymphatic drainage pathways.

terminology.etymology: Afferent means carrying toward a structure.
terminology.notes: Carries lymph into the lymph node.

terminology.etymology: Efferent means carrying away from a structure.
terminology.notes: Carries lymph away from the node, usually through the hilum.

terminology.etymology: Para- means beside or alongside; cortex refers to the outer region.
terminology.notes: The major T-cell-rich region between the cortex and medulla.

terminology.etymology: Named for the relatively tall endothelial cells lining these specialized venules.
terminology.notes: A specialized blood vessel important for entry of naive lymphocytes into lymph nodes.

terminology.etymology: Latin hilum, a small spot or depression where vessels and structures enter or leave an organ.
terminology.notes: The concave region associated with efferent lymphatic and vascular structures.

relations.note: Mature naive T cells generated and selected in the thymus populate secondary lymphoid tissues including lymph nodes.
The lymphoid cells participating in lymph-node responses ultimately derive from hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells.

review_notes: Original synthesis checked against current NCBI/NIH reference material and peer-reviewed reviews. The record separates stable gross/histological anatomy from more detailed descriptions of cellular microenvironments.
